en.title: Physiology: the whole course
en.short: What physiology is, how the course and degree are organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text: These notes teach physiology concepts to students. They are not medical advice, they do not give drug doses, and they do not replace your teachers, textbooks or official guidance. Clinical guidelines change and differ between countries, so check the current national or World Health Organization (WHO) source. Laboratory reference ranges also vary with the method and the laboratory. Never use study notes to diagnose or treat yourself or anyone else. If someone is unwell, seek local clinical help.

sections.heading: What physiology is
sections.text:
Physiology is the study of how living systems work. It asks how cells, tissues, organs and the whole body carry out their functions, and why those functions happen as they do. It draws on chemistry, physics and mathematics, and it overlaps anatomy, which describes structure, and biochemistry, which describes molecules.

Physiology usually starts with normal function. Its central idea is homeostasis, the maintenance of a stable internal environment. Understanding the normal state makes it easier to see what changes in disease. The subject is studied as its own degree and also as a major part of medicine, nursing, pharmacy, physiotherapy and other health courses.

sections.heading: How the course and degree are organised
sections.text:
This course has three stages. The introductory stage builds the tools: scientific method and measurement, chemistry and physics, cell structure, homeostasis, membranes, nerves, muscle, body fluids and data handling. The core stage works through the main organ systems and their integration. The master’s stage adds advanced systems, research methods, computational physiology and specialist molecular frontiers.

Degree organisation differs by country and institution. In Nigeria, a BSc Physiology programme commonly lasts four years, but entry route and structure vary, so check your own handbook. In the United Kingdom, a BSc Physiology usually lasts three years, and some programmes include a placement or an integrated master’s year. In the United States, physiology is often studied within a biology or health-related bachelor’s degree. Master’s degrees commonly take one to two years. Always confirm length, awards and regulations with your institution.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory topics come first because later systems depend on them. Measurement and data teach you to judge values and variation. Chemistry and physics explain diffusion, osmosis, electricity and pressure. Cell structure, membranes and membrane potential lead to nerve and muscle physiology. Body fluids and blood introduce the internal environment.

The core topics then follow in a logical order. Cardiovascular, respiratory and renal physiology deal with transport, gas exchange and fluid balance. Acid-base and electrolyte balance follows renal function. Gastrointestinal physiology and metabolism deal with intake and energy. Endocrine physiology explains chemical control. Sensory, motor and autonomic neurophysiology explain nervous control. Haemostasis, immune physiology, reproduction, thermoregulation and exercise show defence, survival and adaptation. Integrative physiology, laboratory methods and ethics, and applied clinical physiology bring the systems together.

At master’s level, the same systems are studied more deeply through advanced systems physiology, research methods, computational and systems physiology, and molecular and cellular frontiers.

sections.heading: How to study physiology
sections.text:
Study for mechanism, not just names. For each system, draw the pathway from stimulus to response: sensor, control centre, effector and feedback. Say aloud why each step happens. Connect systems, for example how the kidneys, blood vessels and hormones act together to control blood pressure.

Use active recall. Close the book and write the pathway or explain it to a classmate. Space your revision over weeks and test yourself with past questions and calculations. Check units and significant figures in every calculation. In the laboratory, learn the purpose of each method, the controls, the ethics and the meaning of a reference range.

Link physiology to disease only after you know the normal function. Use your prescribed textbook and your teacher’s notes, and check current official guidance for any clinical statement.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often memorise lists of facts without the mechanism, so they cannot reason through a new case. Others confuse a normal variation with a disease, or quote a reference range without checking the laboratory and units. Some treat one country’s guideline as universal.

Passive rereading feels productive but is weak. Skipping the introductory topics makes later systems harder. Ignoring mathematics leads to wrong calculations and misread graphs. Finally, do not use course notes to diagnose or treat anyone. These notes teach concepts; clinical care needs a qualified professional.

keyPoints: Physiology explains how the body works from cells to whole systems.
The course moves from foundations to core organ systems and then to master’s-level specialisation.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Learn mechanisms and feedback pathways rather than isolated facts.
Use active recall, spaced revision and careful calculation.
These notes teach concepts and are not medical advice or a treatment guide.

en.title: Scientific method and measurement in physiology
en.short: How physiologists ask testable questions, control variables, use SI units and judge measurement error.

sections.heading: Asking questions
sections.text: Physiologists turn observations into testable questions. A hypothesis is a proposed explanation that can be supported or rejected by measurement. It must be operational: define each variable by the exact procedure used to measure it, such as “heart rate in beats per minute after five minutes seated”. A question that cannot be measured cannot be tested. Good design also states what will be compared and what result would count against the hypothesis.

sections.heading: Variables and controls
sections.text: The independent variable is the factor changed by the researcher. The dependent variable is the response measured. Controlled variables are kept constant because they could otherwise affect the result, for example room temperature or time of day. A control group receives no treatment or a sham procedure, so the effect of the intervention can be separated from normal variation. Repeating measurements reduces random error, and randomising subjects reduces bias. Calibrate every instrument against a known standard before use, and repeat calibration during long sessions.

sections.heading: Units and figures
sections.text: SI base units include metre, kilogram, second, mole and kelvin, with derived units such as pascal for pressure. Some accepted non-SI units remain common in physiology, including litre and millimetre of mercury. Convert to one unit before calculating. Report only significant figures justified by the instrument. For example, heart rates of 72, 76 and 74 beats per minute give a mean of (72 + 76 + 74) ÷ 3 = 74 beats per minute. If the meter reads to the nearest beat, write 74, not 74.0.

sections.heading: Accuracy and error
sections.text: Accuracy is closeness to the true value. Precision is closeness of repeated measurements to one another. A result can be precise but inaccurate if the instrument is wrongly calibrated. Random error scatters results around a value and is reduced by averaging repeats. Systematic error shifts all results in one direction, as with a blocked pressure line, and is not removed by repeating. Biological variation, observer bias and environmental change are further sources. State the likely error and do not overstate small differences.

keyPoints: A testable hypothesis needs operational definitions of every variable.
The independent variable is changed, the dependent variable is measured, and controlled variables are kept constant.
Control groups, randomisation and repeated measurements help separate a real effect from normal variation and bias.
Calibrate instruments against a known standard before use and repeat calibration during long sessions.
Use SI units, convert to one unit before calculating, and report only significant figures the instrument supports.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value, precision is closeness between repeats, random error scatters results, systematic error shifts them, and mean = sum of values ÷ number of values.

en.title: Chemistry and physics foundations for physiology
en.short: Water, ions, pH and buffers; diffusion, osmosis and gas laws; energy, enzymes and measurement.

sections.heading: Water and ions
sections.text: Water is polar. Hydrogen bonds give it high heat capacity and make it a good solvent for ions and polar molecules. Ions are charged particles. Electrolytes dissociate into ions in water. Concentration is usually mol/L or mmol/L. Osmolarity is total solute particles per litre; it predicts water movement. Viscosity is resistance to flow; blood viscosity depends mainly on haematocrit, the fraction of blood volume occupied by red cells, and on plasma proteins.

sections.heading: pH and buffers
sections.text: pH measures hydrogen ion concentration: pH = −log10[H+]. A low pH means more H+ and more acidity. A buffer is a weak acid and its conjugate base that resists pH change. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log10([A−]/[HA]), where pKa is the pH at which the acid is half dissociated. Worked example: if pKa = 6.1 and [A−]/[HA] = 20, log10(20) = 1.30, so pH = 6.1 + 1.30 = 7.40. Buffers work best near their pKa.

sections.heading: Diffusion and gases
sections.text: Diffusion is net movement of particles from high to low concentration. Osmosis is water movement across a semipermeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration. Osmotic pressure can be estimated by π = iCRT, where i is the number of particles each solute unit forms in solution, C concentration, R the gas constant and T absolute temperature. Boyle’s law: P1V1 = P2V2 at constant temperature. Example: 2 L at 100 kPa compressed to 1 L gives 200 kPa. Dalton’s law sums partial pressures; Henry’s law says dissolved gas is proportional to partial pressure.

sections.heading: Energy and measurement
sections.text: Energy is the capacity to do work. Gibbs free energy is the energy available to do work. A reaction is spontaneous when its Gibbs free energy change is negative. Enzymes are biological catalysts. They lower activation energy and speed reactions without changing the overall energy change. Michaelis-Menten kinetics: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), where [S] is substrate concentration, Vmax is maximum rate and Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax. Physiological measurement converts a physical quantity into a signal, often electrical. Examples include pH electrodes, pressure transducers, spirometers and spectrophotometers. Calibrate with known standards, use SI units, and check accuracy and precision. Signal drift and noise limit measurement.

keyPoints: Water is polar, with high heat capacity and solvent power; electrolytes are ions in solution.
pH = −log10[H+] and buffers resist pH change, working best near their pKa.
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log10([A−]/[HA]).
Osmotic pressure π = iCRT; osmosis is water movement across a semipermeable membrane.
Boyle’s law: P1V1 = P2V2 at constant temperature; Dalton and Henry laws describe gas mixtures and dissolved gas.
A negative Gibbs free energy change means a reaction is spontaneous; enzymes lower activation energy; Michaelis-Menten v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); calibrate instruments before measurement.

en.title: Cell structure and function
en.short: How the plasma membrane, organelles, cytoskeleton and junctions support cell function and tissue organisation.

sections.heading: Membrane and organelles
sections.text: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins and cholesterol. It is selectively permeable: small nonpolar molecules cross easily, while ions and polar molecules need channels, carriers or vesicles. The nucleus holds DNA. Mitochondria produce ATP, the cell’s energy currency. The rough endoplasmic reticulum (ER) makes proteins for secretion or membranes, and the smooth ER makes lipids and stores calcium. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles. Lysosomes contain enzymes that digest material.

sections.heading: Cytoskeleton and junctions
sections.text: The cytoskeleton is a network of protein filaments. Microfilaments (actin) support shape and movement. Intermediate filaments give mechanical strength. Microtubules form tracks for vesicle movement and make up cilia and the spindle. Cell junctions connect cells. Tight junctions seal the space between cells and help keep apical and basolateral surfaces separate. Adherens junctions and desmosomes anchor cells to each other. Gap junctions allow small molecules and ions to pass between cells. Hemidesmosomes anchor epithelium to basement membrane.

sections.heading: Secretion and signalling
sections.text: Secretion depends on structure. A protein made in the rough ER travels to the Golgi, is packaged in a vesicle, and is released when the vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane. This is exocytosis. Signalling also depends on membrane proteins: receptors bind hormones or transmitters and pass the message inside. Gap junctions let coupled cells share signals quickly. The cytoskeleton positions organelles and guides vesicles, so the cell can direct secretion to one surface.

sections.heading: Tissue organisation
sections.text: Epithelial cells are polarised: one surface faces a lumen or outside, the other rests on basement membrane. Junctions and cytoskeleton hold this arrangement. In a teaching lab in Ibadan, Amina compares a mucus-secreting airway cell with a muscle cell. The airway cell has many Golgi stacks and secretory vesicles; its tight junctions separate the mucus release side from the blood side. The muscle cell has more contractile filaments. Structure predicts function.

keyPoints: The plasma membrane is a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer with proteins.
Rough ER and Golgi package proteins for secretion; mitochondria supply ATP.
The cytoskeleton includes actin microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules.
Tight junctions seal cells, desmosomes anchor cells, and gap junctions allow small molecule passage.
Cell polarity and junctions organise epithelia into tissues.
Secretory cells have abundant ER and Golgi, and vesicles release by exocytosis.

en.title: Homeostasis and control systems
en.short: How set points, feedback, feed-forward and compartments keep internal conditions stable.

sections.heading: Set points
sections.text:
Homeostasis is the maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment. A set point is the reference value, or narrow range, that a control system aims to keep. It is not always fixed: it can change with sleep, exercise, age and disease.

Core temperature, for example, is usually near 37°C but varies slightly through the day. A control system has sensors that detect a variable, a control centre that compares it with the set point, and effectors that produce the response. Stability does not mean no change; it means change is kept within limits.

sections.heading: Feedback loops
sections.text:
Negative feedback is the main mechanism. A deviation from the set point triggers a response that opposes the deviation. If a variable rises, the response lowers it; if it falls, the response raises it. This is like a thermostat.

Positive feedback amplifies a deviation. It is less common in steady states and usually has an endpoint. Childbirth and blood clotting are standard examples: the process drives itself forward until the baby is delivered or the clot is formed. Without an endpoint, positive feedback can be harmful.

sections.heading: Feed-forward and compartments
sections.text:
Feed-forward control starts a response before the disturbance arrives, using anticipation. Salivation before food, or a rise in heart rate before exercise, are examples.

Body fluids are divided into compartments: intracellular fluid inside cells, and extracellular fluid outside them, including plasma and interstitial fluid. Membranes separate these compartments, and exchange between them is controlled. Homeostasis therefore regulates both the composition of each compartment and the movement between them.

sections.heading: Nervous and endocrine
sections.text:
The nervous and endocrine systems work together. Nervous control is fast and short-lived, using nerve impulses and neurotransmitters. Endocrine control is slower and longer-lasting, using hormones carried in the blood. The hypothalamus links the two and coordinates homeostatic responses.

For example, Amina drinks little water on a hot day. Her extracellular fluid becomes slightly concentrated. Sensors detect this, the brain increases thirst and reduces water loss, and she drinks. The deviation is corrected.

keyPoints: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions within limits around set points.
Negative feedback opposes a deviation and is the main steady-state control.
Positive feedback amplifies a deviation and usually needs an endpoint.
Feed-forward control anticipates a disturbance and acts before it.
Body fluids are separated into intracellular and extracellular compartments.
Nervous control is fast and short; endocrine control is slower and longer; the hypothalamus links them.

en.title: Membrane transport and membrane potential
en.short: Diffusion, osmosis, facilitated and active transport, cotransport, equilibrium potentials and resting membrane potential.

sections.heading: Passive transport
sections.text: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from high to low concentration, driven by random thermal motion; it needs no ATP. Osmosis is water diffusion across a semipermeable membrane from low solute concentration to high solute concentration. Facilitated transport uses membrane proteins to move polar or large solutes down their gradient, without ATP. Channels form pores; carriers change shape. For example, glucose enters cells by facilitated transport.

sections.heading: Active transport and cotransport
sections.text: Active transport moves solutes against a gradient and needs energy. The Na+-K+ pump is primary active transport: it uses one ATP to move 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in. This keeps Na+ high outside and K+ high inside. Cotransport is a type of secondary active transport: it uses one ion’s downhill gradient to move another solute uphill. For example, Na+-glucose cotransport in the intestine uses the Na+ gradient to absorb glucose.

sections.heading: Equilibrium potentials
sections.text: An equilibrium potential is the membrane voltage at which an ion’s electrical and chemical forces balance, so net flux is zero. The Nernst equation estimates it: E = (61/z) log10([ion]out/[ion]in) mV at 37°C, where z is the ion’s charge. Worked example: if K+ is 5 mM outside and 140 mM inside, E_K = 61 × log10(5/140) = 61 × (−1.447) = −88 mV. For Na+, with high outside and low inside, E_Na is positive, about +60 mV.

sections.heading: Resting membrane potential
sections.text: The resting membrane potential (RMP) is the voltage across a cell membrane at rest. The Na+-K+ pump maintains gradients, and leak channels make the membrane more permeable to K+ than Na+. K+ leaves down its gradient, leaving negative charge inside, until the membrane approaches E_K. Na+ leak slightly offsets this, so RMP is less negative than E_K, often about −70 mV. Values vary by cell and must be measured.

keyPoints: Diffusion and osmosis are passive and need no ATP; osmosis is water movement across a semipermeable membrane.
Facilitated transport uses membrane proteins to move solutes down their gradient without ATP.
The Na+-K+ pump uses ATP to move 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, maintaining the ion gradients.
Cotransport uses one ion’s downhill gradient to move another solute uphill.
The Nernst equation E = (61/z) log10([ion]out/[ion]in) mV at 37°C gives an ion’s equilibrium potential.
Resting membrane potential is close to E_K because resting membranes are more permeable to K+ than Na+, often about −70 mV.

en.title: Nerve cells and action potentials
en.short: Neuron structure, graded potentials, action potentials, synapses and simple circuits.

sections.heading: Neurons and graded signals
sections.text: A neuron has a cell body, dendrites, an axon and synaptic terminals. Dendrites receive inputs; the axon carries output. The axon hillock is the trigger zone, and myelin sheaths with nodes of Ranvier speed conduction. Graded potentials are local changes in membrane potential that fade with distance. They arise at dendrites or sensory endings and can add together, called summation. Excitatory inputs depolarise the membrane; inhibitory inputs hyperpolarise it. Threshold is the membrane potential at which an action potential starts. If summed depolarisation reaches it at the axon hillock, firing begins. Resting potential −70 mV plus graded depolarisation 15 mV gives −55 mV. If threshold is −55 mV, the action potential begins.

sections.heading: Action potential phases
sections.text: An action potential is a brief, all-or-none electrical signal. At threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium enters, causing depolarisation that often overshoots zero. Sodium channels then inactivate. Voltage-gated potassium channels open and potassium leaves, causing repolarisation. The membrane may briefly hyperpolarise before returning to rest. The absolute refractory period prevents another action potential; the relative refractory period needs a stronger stimulus. Propagation occurs along the axon. In unmyelinated axons it is continuous. In myelinated axons it jumps between nodes of Ranvier, called saltatory conduction, which is faster and energy-efficient. The action potential does not decrease in size as it travels.

sections.heading: Synapses and circuits
sections.text: A chemical synapse transmits signals between neurons. An action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal, calcium enters, and neurotransmitter vesicles release their contents. The neurotransmitter crosses the synaptic cleft and binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. This produces an excitatory postsynaptic potential, which depolarises, or an inhibitory postsynaptic potential, which hyperpolarises. Acetylcholine, glutamate, GABA, dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline are examples. Postsynaptic potentials summate; if threshold is reached, the next neuron fires. Simple circuits include divergence, where one neuron signals many, and convergence, where many signal one. In a stretch reflex, a sensory neuron excites a motor neuron directly, while an inhibitory interneuron reduces activity in the opposing muscle.

keyPoints: A neuron has dendrites for input, an axon for output, and a trigger zone at the axon hillock.
Graded potentials are local and decremental; they summate and can reach threshold.
Resting potential −70 mV plus graded depolarisation 15 mV gives −55 mV; if threshold is −55 mV, firing begins.
An action potential is all-or-none: sodium enters during depolarisation and potassium leaves during repolarisation.
Myelinated axons conduct by saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier, which is faster than continuous conduction.
Chemical synapses release neurotransmitter after calcium entry, and excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials summate.

en.title: Muscle physiology: contraction and movement
en.short: How skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle contract, and how motor units and fatigue shape movement.

sections.heading: Sarcomere and sliding filaments
sections.text: A skeletal muscle fibre is a long cell containing myofibrils. The sarcomere is the repeating unit between two Z lines. It holds thick filaments of myosin and thin filaments of actin. In the sliding filament model, contraction shortens the sarcomere as thin filaments slide over thick ones. The A band stays the same length; the I band and H zone narrow. Titin helps keep the filaments aligned and gives elastic recoil.

sections.heading: Excitation and cross-bridges
sections.text: A motor neuron releases acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter, at the neuromuscular junction. This depolarises the muscle fibre, and the action potential spreads along the sarcolemma (surface membrane) and into T tubules (transverse tubules). Excitation-contraction coupling is the link between the electrical signal and contraction. It releases calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, the calcium store. Calcium binds troponin on the thin filament, moving tropomyosin and exposing myosin-binding sites. Cross-bridge cycling follows: myosin binds actin, the power stroke pulls the thin filament, and ATP allows detachment and re-cocking. Without calcium, tropomyosin blocks the sites and the muscle relaxes.

sections.heading: Cardiac and smooth muscle
sections.text: Cardiac muscle is striated and branched, with intercalated discs, which join cells, and gap junctions that let excitation spread. Its contraction depends on calcium entering through L-type channels and triggering calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, called calcium-induced calcium release. Smooth muscle is not striated. Calcium binds the protein calmodulin, activating myosin light-chain kinase, which phosphorylates myosin. Smooth muscle contracts slowly and can sustain tone. It is controlled by nerves, hormones and stretch.

sections.heading: Motor units and fatigue
sections.text: A motor unit is one motor neuron and the muscle fibres it supplies. Small units control fine movements; large units produce force. More units are recruited as effort rises. Amina lifting a bucket recruits more motor units than holding a pen. Muscle fatigue is a fall in force with sustained activity. It has several causes, including metabolite accumulation, impaired calcium handling and failure of excitation. It differs from central fatigue, which starts in the nervous system. Rest and recovery restore performance.

keyPoints: The sarcomere is the repeating contractile unit between Z lines, with myosin thick filaments and actin thin filaments.
Excitation-contraction coupling links the muscle action potential to calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Calcium exposes myosin-binding sites on actin, allowing cross-bridge cycling, which uses ATP.
Cardiac muscle uses calcium-induced calcium release and gap junctions; smooth muscle uses calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase.
A motor unit is one motor neuron and its fibres; recruitment increases force.
Muscle fatigue is multifactorial and differs from central fatigue.

en.title: Body fluids and blood: composition and functions
en.short: Body fluid compartments, plasma, blood cells and haematocrit.

sections.heading: Fluid compartments
sections.text: Total body water is about 60% of body mass in a healthy adult, but this varies with age, sex and body fat. It is divided into intracellular fluid (ICF), the water inside cells, and extracellular fluid (ECF), the water outside cells. ICF is about two thirds of total body water; ECF is about one third and includes interstitial fluid and plasma. Water moves by osmosis, so it follows solute concentration. Sodium is the main ECF cation and potassium the main ICF cation. The cell membrane and capillary wall keep the compartments different in composition.

sections.heading: Plasma composition
sections.text: Plasma is the liquid part of blood. It is about 90% water and contains plasma proteins, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones and waste products. Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and helps hold water in the capillaries by oncotic pressure. Globulins include antibodies and transport proteins. Fibrinogen is used in clotting. Plasma also carries glucose, lipids, amino acids, urea and carbon dioxide. Its electrolyte pattern resembles interstitial fluid, but plasma has more protein.

sections.heading: Blood cells and haematocrit
sections.text: Red cells, or erythrocytes, are biconcave and packed with haemoglobin, which carries oxygen. They lack a nucleus in adult mammals and last about 120 days. White cells, or leukocytes, defend the body; they include granulocytes, which have granules in their cytoplasm, and agranulocytes, such as lymphocytes and monocytes. Platelets are small cell fragments that help stop bleeding. Haematocrit is the fraction of blood volume occupied by red cells after centrifugation. It is commonly about 0.40 to 0.50 in men and a little lower in women; values also differ with altitude and pregnancy. For example, if blood volume is 5 L and haematocrit is 0.45, plasma volume is 5 × (1 − 0.45) = 2.75 L. Check local reference ranges.

keyPoints: Total body water is divided into intracellular and extracellular compartments.
Sodium is the main extracellular cation; potassium is the main intracellular cation.
Plasma is mostly water and contains proteins, electrolytes, nutrients and wastes.
Albumin helps maintain oncotic pressure and keep water in capillaries.
Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin; white cells defend the body; platelets help haemostasis.
Haematocrit is the red cell fraction of blood; plasma volume = blood volume × (1 − haematocrit).

en.title: Mathematics and data in physiology
en.short: Units, dilution, clearance, flow, Fick principle, graphs, descriptive statistics and variability.

sections.heading: Units and concentration
sections.text:
Physiology uses SI units: metre, kilogram, second, mole and kelvin. Derived units include pascal (Pa) and joule (J); the litre (L) is a non-SI unit accepted for use with SI. Concentration is solute amount per volume. Molar concentration is mol/L; mass concentration is g/L; percentage concentration is often g per 100 mL. Osmolarity is osmoles per litre of solution.

Convert to one unit before comparing: 1 g = 1,000 mg and 1 L = 1,000 mL. A value without a unit is incomplete.

sections.heading: Dilution and clearance
sections.text:
Dilution conserves solute amount: C1V1 = C2V2. If 10 mL of 0.5 mol/L solution is made up to 100 mL, C2 = (0.5 × 10) ÷ 100 = 0.05 mol/L.

Clearance is the plasma volume cleared of a substance per unit time: clearance = (U × V) ÷ P, where U is urine concentration, V is urine flow and P is plasma concentration. U and P need the same unit. Clearance is a volume per time, not the mass excreted.

sections.heading: Flow and Fick
sections.text:
Flow is volume moved per time, such as L/min. Flow depends on pressure difference and resistance: flow = pressure difference ÷ resistance. The Fick principle says uptake or release of a substance equals blood flow times the arteriovenous concentration difference.

For oxygen: cardiac output = oxygen consumption ÷ (arterial O2 content − mixed venous O2 content). If consumption is 250 mL/min and the difference is 200 − 150 = 50 mL/L, output = 250 ÷ 50 = 5 L/min. Keep units consistent.

sections.heading: Graphs and variability
sections.text:
Plot data with labelled axes, units and a clear scale. Use a line graph for continuous change and a scatter plot for two variables. Slope is a rate; area under some curves is total amount.

Descriptive statistics summarise data: mean, median, range and standard deviation (SD). SD describes spread of observations; standard error of the mean (SEM) describes uncertainty of a mean and is smaller. Variability can be biological variation, measurement error or sampling variation. Report n and the statistic used.

keyPoints: Convert all measurements to consistent SI units before calculating.
Dilution follows C1V1 = C2V2.
Clearance = (U × V) ÷ P; it is a volume per time.
Flow = pressure difference ÷ resistance; Fick principle: uptake = blood flow × arteriovenous concentration difference.
Cardiac output by Fick = oxygen consumption ÷ arteriovenous oxygen difference.
SD describes spread of observations; SEM describes uncertainty of a mean and is smaller.

en.title: Cardiovascular physiology
en.short: Heart electrical activity, cardiac cycle, output, ECG, haemodynamics and blood pressure control.

sections.heading: Cardiac muscle and pacemakers
sections.text: Cardiac muscle is striated, branched and joined by intercalated discs. Gap junctions let current pass between cells, so the heart behaves as a functional syncytium. Its action potential has a long plateau caused by calcium entry, which helps contraction and prevents tetanus. Pacemaker cells in the sinoatrial node have an unstable resting potential and depolarise slowly; they set the resting heart rate. Autonomic nerves and hormones adjust this rate.

sections.heading: Cardiac cycle and output
sections.text: The cardiac cycle is one heartbeat: the ventricles fill, atrial contraction completes the filling, then the ventricles contract and eject blood, then relax. Stroke volume (SV) is the volume ejected per beat, equal to end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume. Cardiac output (CO) is SV times heart rate. Frank-Starling relation: within limits, greater ventricular filling stretches muscle and increases force, so SV rises. Contractility (the force of contraction at a given filling) and afterload (the pressure the ventricle ejects against) also affect SV. Example: heart rate 70 beats/min and SV 70 mL give CO = 70 × 70 = 4,900 mL/min, about 4.9 L/min.

sections.heading: ECG basics
sections.text: An electrocardiogram records electrical activity at the body surface. The P wave is atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation, and the T wave is ventricular repolarisation. The ECG shows timing and rhythm, not the force of contraction. A normal rhythm starts in the sinoatrial node; abnormal rhythms arise from other pacemakers or conduction blocks.

sections.heading: Haemodynamics and blood pressure
sections.text: Haemodynamics studies blood flow. Flow equals pressure difference divided by resistance. Mean arterial pressure is approximately cardiac output times total peripheral resistance. Resistance rises when vessels narrow; Poiseuille’s law says resistance is inversely proportional to radius to the fourth power. Microcirculation is exchange across capillary walls by diffusion and filtration. Venous return depends on the pressure gradient, valves, skeletal muscle pump and breathing. Local blood flow is matched to tissue need by autoregulation, metabolic vasodilation and endothelial signals. Short-term blood pressure control uses baroreceptors, stretch sensors in the large arteries; long-term control depends on blood volume.

keyPoints: Cardiac muscle behaves as a syncytium because gap junctions spread current between cells.
The sinoatrial node is the normal pacemaker and sets heart rate.
Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume; for example 70 beats/min × 70 mL = 4,900 mL/min.
Frank-Starling relation: greater filling increases stroke volume within physiological limits.
ECG waves: P = atrial depolarisation, QRS = ventricular depolarisation, T = ventricular repolarisation.
Mean arterial pressure is approximately cardiac output × total peripheral resistance, and resistance depends strongly on vessel radius.

en.title: Respiratory physiology and gas exchange
en.short: Breathing mechanics, lung volumes, alveolar ventilation, diffusion, haemoglobin, CO2 transport and control.

sections.heading: Mechanics and volumes
sections.text: Breathing is pressure driven. The diaphragm and external intercostals expand the thorax, pleural pressure falls, and air flows into the alveoli. Quiet expiration is passive. Compliance is change in lung volume per unit pressure change (ΔV/ΔP): high compliance means easy inflation, but very high compliance can reduce elastic recoil. Airway resistance is pressure gradient divided by flow; resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius, so narrowing has a large effect. Lung volumes include tidal, inspiratory reserve, expiratory reserve and residual volumes. Vital capacity is the maximum volume exhaled after a full breath in. Spirometry cannot measure residual volume.

sections.heading: Ventilation and diffusion
sections.text: Alveolar ventilation is fresh air reaching alveoli per minute: VA = (VT − VD) × f, where VT is tidal volume, VD is dead space (air not taking part in gas exchange) and f is breaths per minute. Example: VT 500 mL, VD 150 mL, f 12/min, so VA = (500 − 150) × 12 = 350 × 12 = 4,200 mL/min, or 4.2 L/min. Diffusion follows Fick’s law: rate is proportional to surface area and partial pressure gradient, and inversely proportional to thickness. Carbon dioxide diffuses 20 times more readily than oxygen.

sections.heading: Blood gas transport
sections.text: Oxygen is carried mainly bound to haemoglobin. The oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid and depends on partial pressure of oxygen. Affinity falls when pH falls, PCO2 rises, temperature rises or 2,3-BPG (2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, a red blood cell metabolite) rises; this shifts the curve right and releases oxygen to tissues. Oxygen content depends on haemoglobin concentration, saturation and dissolved oxygen. Carbon dioxide is carried mostly as bicarbonate, with smaller amounts dissolved and bound to haemoglobin. The Haldane effect means deoxygenated blood carries more CO2.

sections.heading: Control of breathing
sections.text: Breathing is generated in the medulla, with input from the pons. Central chemoreceptors respond to hydrogen ions in cerebrospinal fluid, which rise when arterial PCO2 rises. Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies respond to low arterial PO2, especially below 60 mmHg, and to PCO2 and pH. Chemical control keeps arterial PCO2 and pH stable.

keyPoints: Breathing is pressure driven: the diaphragm and external intercostals expand the thorax, and quiet expiration is passive.
Compliance = ΔV/ΔP; airway resistance = ΔP/flow, and resistance rises sharply as airway radius falls.
Alveolar ventilation VA = (VT − VD) × f; with VT 500 mL, VD 150 mL and f 12/min, VA = 4.2 L/min.
Diffusion follows Fick’s law and is proportional to area and partial pressure gradient and inversely proportional to thickness.
Oxygen content (mL/dL) = (Hb × 1.34 × SaO2) + (0.003 × PaO2), where Hb is g/dL, SaO2 is a fraction and PaO2 is in mmHg.
Central chemoreceptors sense CSF hydrogen ions from CO2; peripheral chemoreceptors sense low PO2, high PCO2 and low pH.

en.title: Renal physiology and urine formation
en.short: Nephron, filtration, reabsorption, secretion, countercurrent concentration, and control of sodium, water, K and GFR.

sections.heading: Nephron and filtration
sections.text:
The nephron is the kidney’s functional unit. It has a renal corpuscle (glomerulus plus Bowman’s capsule), then proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule and collecting duct. Filtration occurs in the corpuscle: glomerular blood pressure pushes water and small solutes through the filtration barrier, while cells and large proteins remain in blood.

Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is filtrate formed per minute. GFR = Kf × net filtration pressure, where Kf is the filtration coefficient. Inulin clearance measures GFR because inulin is filtered but not reabsorbed or secreted: GFR = (urine inulin × urine flow) ÷ plasma inulin. Example: 100 mg/mL × 1.0 mL/min ÷ 1.0 mg/mL = 100 mL/min. GFR is regulated by the myogenic response, tubuloglomerular feedback from the macula densa, sympathetic nerves and angiotensin II.

sections.heading: Reabsorption and secretion
sections.text:
Most filtrate is reabsorbed. The proximal tubule reabsorbs about two thirds of filtered sodium and water, plus glucose and amino acids by cotransport, and secretes hydrogen ions and organic acids. The loop of Henle creates the medullary gradient: its descending limb is permeable to water, while the ascending limb is impermeable to water and actively transports sodium, potassium and chloride.

The distal tubule and collecting duct fine-tune the final urine. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases water permeability by inserting aquaporins. Secretion means moving substances from blood into tubular fluid, as with potassium and hydrogen ions.

sections.heading: Countercurrent multiplication
sections.text:
Countercurrent multiplication builds a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium. Fluid flows in opposite directions in the two limbs of the loop. Water leaves the descending limb, and the ascending limb pumps out sodium chloride while staying impermeable to water. The effect repeats along the loop, so osmolality rises toward the renal papilla. Vasa recta countercurrent exchange preserves this gradient.

ADH controls the final step. When ADH is high, collecting ducts become water-permeable and water is reabsorbed, producing concentrated urine. When ADH is low, ducts stay relatively impermeable and dilute urine is produced.

keyPoints: The nephron includes the renal corpuscle, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule and collecting duct.
GFR = Kf × net filtration pressure, and inulin clearance measures GFR as (urine inulin × urine flow) ÷ plasma inulin.
Most filtered sodium and water is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, while secretion moves substances from blood into tubular fluid.
Countercurrent multiplication in the loop of Henle creates a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium.
ADH increases collecting duct water permeability, and aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.
GFR is regulated by myogenic autoregulation, tubuloglomerular feedback, sympathetic nerves and angiotensin II.

en.title: Acid-base and electrolyte balance
en.short: Buffers, Henderson-Hasselbalch, respiratory and renal pH control, acidosis and alkalosis, and electrolyte balance.

sections.heading: Buffers and pH
sections.text:
pH is −log10[H+], so a small pH change means a large change in hydrogen ion concentration. A buffer is a weak acid and its conjugate base that resists pH change by taking up or releasing H+.

The main extracellular buffer is bicarbonate (HCO3−) with carbonic acid (H2CO3). Phosphate buffers work inside cells and in urine. Proteins, especially haemoglobin, also buffer H+.

sections.heading: Henderson-Hasselbalch
sections.text:
The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation links pH to the bicarbonate and carbon dioxide pair: pH = pKa + log([HCO3−] ÷ (0.03 × PaCO2)), where PaCO2 is the arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide. For carbonic acid pKa is about 6.1, and 0.03 is the solubility of CO2 in mmol/L per mmHg.

Example: if HCO3− is 24 mmol/L and PaCO2 is 40 mmHg, dissolved CO2 is 0.03 × 40 = 1.2 mmol/L. The ratio is 24 ÷ 1.2 = 20, log10 20 = 1.30, so pH = 6.1 + 1.30 = 7.40. The 20:1 ratio is the normal reference point.

sections.heading: Respiratory and renal control
sections.text:
Chemoreceptors sense pH and CO2. Ventilation controls PaCO2: hypoventilation raises CO2 and lowers pH, while hyperventilation lowers CO2 and raises pH. This respiratory response is fast.

The kidneys act slowly, over hours to days. They reabsorb filtered HCO3−, secrete H+ and generate new HCO3−. Aldosterone increases H+ secretion and sodium reabsorption. Renal compensation changes plasma HCO3−, the metabolic component.

sections.heading: Acidosis, alkalosis and electrolytes
sections.text:
Acidosis lowers pH; alkalosis raises it. Metabolic acidosis has low HCO3−, from diarrhoea, renal failure, ketoacidosis or lactic acidosis. Metabolic alkalosis has high HCO3−, from vomiting or diuretics. Respiratory acidosis is hypoventilation; respiratory alkalosis is hyperventilation.

Compensation opposes the primary change but does not fully correct pH. Sodium is the main extracellular cation; potassium is mainly intracellular. Chloride is the main extracellular anion. Calcium, phosphate and magnesium are also balanced. The kidneys and hormones regulate electrolyte output. Clinical management follows current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: pH = −log10[H+]; normal arterial pH is about 7.35 to 7.45.
The bicarbonate buffer is described by pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3−] ÷ (0.03 × PaCO2)).
At HCO3− 24 mmol/L and PaCO2 40 mmHg, the ratio is 20 and pH is about 7.40.
Lungs change PaCO2 quickly; kidneys change HCO3− slowly.
Metabolic acidosis lowers HCO3−; metabolic alkalosis raises it; respiratory disorders change PaCO2.
Sodium is mainly extracellular, potassium mainly intracellular, and the kidneys regulate electrolyte balance.

en.title: Gastrointestinal physiology and digestion
en.short: Motility, secretion, digestion and absorption, plus liver, biliary, pancreatic and gut control.

sections.heading: Motility
sections.text: The gut wall has mucosa, submucosa, muscle and serosa. Motility mixes food with secretions and moves it forward. Peristalsis is a wave of contraction behind a bolus, the swallowed mass, that pushes it along. Segmentation is rhythmic contraction of circular muscle that mixes chyme, the partly digested food, without net forward movement. Sphincters act as valves, preventing reflux and controlling emptying. Between meals, the migrating motor complex, a fasting sweep, clears the stomach and small intestine.

sections.heading: Secretion and organs
sections.text: Saliva moistens food and its amylase begins starch digestion. Parietal cells in the stomach secrete acid and intrinsic factor; chief cells secrete pepsinogen, which acid activates to pepsin. Acid also kills many microbes. The exocrine pancreas releases bicarbonate, which neutralises chyme, and enzymes for starch, fat and protein. The liver makes bile, and the gallbladder stores it. Bile salts emulsify fat into small droplets.

sections.heading: Digestion and absorption
sections.text: Digestion breaks polymers into absorbable units. Carbohydrates become monosaccharides; proteins become amino acids and small peptides; fats become fatty acids and monoglycerides. Villi and brush-border enzymes increase surface area and complete digestion. Fat products and bile salts form micelles, tiny bile-salt particles. The fat products are absorbed mainly in the jejunum, then packaged into chylomicrons, fat-carrying particles. The ileum mainly reabsorbs bile salts and absorbs vitamin B12. The colon absorbs water and electrolytes and houses bacteria that ferment fibre.

sections.heading: Control and feeding
sections.text: Gut function is controlled by the enteric nervous system, a local network in the wall, and by parasympathetic nerves, mainly the vagus, which increase secretion and motility. Sympathetic activity inhibits these functions. Hormones coordinate the organs. Gastrin stimulates acid secretion. Secretin stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate. Cholecystokinin (CCK) stimulates pancreatic enzymes and gallbladder contraction and slows gastric emptying. GLP-1 promotes satiety, the feeling of fullness, and ghrelin stimulates hunger. The hypothalamus integrates feeding signals. For example, after Amina eats a fatty meal, CCK slows her stomach and sends bile and enzymes to the intestine.

keyPoints: Motility uses peristalsis to propel and segmentation to mix; sphincters control flow.
Gastric acid activates pepsin and kills microbes; intrinsic factor is needed for vitamin B12 absorption.
Pancreatic bicarbonate neutralises acid, and pancreatic enzymes digest starch, fat and protein.
Bile salts emulsify fat; fat absorption occurs mainly in the jejunum via micelles and chylomicrons.
The enteric nervous system and vagus stimulate gut function; sympathetic activity inhibits it.
Gastrin, secretin, CCK, GLP-1 and ghrelin link gut function to feeding control.

en.title: Metabolism and energy balance
en.short: How cells make ATP, how we measure energy use, and how the body stores and mobilises fuel.

sections.heading: Cellular energy production
sections.text:
Cells use adenosine triphosphate (ATP) as the energy currency. Glycolysis breaks glucose to pyruvate in the cytoplasm, yielding a small amount of ATP. With oxygen, pyruvate enters mitochondria and the Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation produces most ATP. Without oxygen, pyruvate becomes lactate and less ATP is made.

Fats and amino acids also enter these pathways. The respiratory quotient (RQ) is carbon dioxide produced divided by oxygen used; it is about 0.8 on a mixed diet, near 1.0 for carbohydrate and 0.7 for fat.

sections.heading: Measuring energy use
sections.text:
Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the energy used at rest, awake, after an overnight fast, in a neutral environment. It is the largest part of daily expenditure and depends mainly on lean body mass, age, sex and thyroid status.

Calorimetry measures energy use. Direct calorimetry measures heat loss. Indirect calorimetry estimates it from oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production. For example, using 0.25 L of oxygen per minute and about 4.8 kcal per litre gives 0.25 × 4.8 = 1.2 kcal/min, or 1.2 × 1,440 = 1,728 kcal/day. The value is approximate because energy per litre varies.

sections.heading: Fed and fasted states
sections.text:
After a meal, the fed state dominates. Insulin rises and promotes storage: glucose becomes glycogen in liver and muscle, and excess energy becomes fat in adipose tissue.

In the fasted state, insulin falls and glucagon rises. The liver releases glucose from glycogen (glycogenolysis) and makes glucose from amino acids and glycerol (gluconeogenesis). Adipose tissue releases fatty acids (lipolysis), and the liver makes ketone bodies for the brain.

sections.heading: Hormonal control
sections.text:
Energy balance is intake minus expenditure. Insulin is the main storage hormone. Glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol mobilise fuel.

Leptin, made by adipose tissue, signals fat stores and reduces appetite. Ghrelin, from the stomach, rises before meals and increases appetite. Thyroid hormones set the pace of metabolism. These signals act on the hypothalamus, which controls hunger and satiety. Body weight is regulated by feedback, not by willpower alone.

keyPoints: ATP is the cell’s energy currency; oxidative phosphorylation makes most of it when oxygen is available.
BMR is resting energy use after an overnight fast, measured by calorimetry.
Indirect calorimetry estimates energy use from oxygen consumption; energy used = oxygen used × energy per litre (about 4.8 kcal/L on a mixed diet).
RQ = CO2 produced ÷ O2 used; it is about 0.8 on a mixed diet.
Insulin stores fuel after meals; glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol mobilise it during fasting.
Leptin and ghrelin act on the hypothalamus to influence appetite and energy balance.

en.title: Endocrine physiology: hormones and feedback
en.short: Hormone synthesis, transport, receptors, and the main endocrine axes and feedback loops.

sections.heading: Hormone basics
sections.text: Hormones are chemical signals secreted into blood to act on distant cells. Peptide hormones are made as precursor proteins and stored; amines come from tyrosine; steroids are made from cholesterol and are not stored. Peptides and most amines (such as adrenaline) are water-soluble, so they travel free and act on surface receptors, often via second messengers (internal signals). Steroids and thyroid hormone are lipid-soluble, travel bound to carrier proteins such as albumin, and act on intracellular receptors to change gene transcription. Only free hormone is active. For example, if total cortisol is 500 nmol/L and 98% is bound, free cortisol is 2% × 500 = 10 nmol/L.

sections.heading: Hypothalamic-pituitary axes
sections.text: The hypothalamus releases releasing or inhibiting hormones into portal blood to the anterior pituitary. The pituitary releases hormones that stimulate target glands. For example, thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) stimulates thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which stimulates T3 and T4. Negative feedback from target hormones restrains the axis. Growth hormone (GH) is controlled by growth-hormone-releasing hormone and somatostatin; GH acts partly through insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). The posterior pituitary stores antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin, made in the hypothalamus.

sections.heading: Thyroid and adrenal
sections.text: Thyroid hormones T3 and T4 raise basal metabolic rate and support growth and development. Most circulating T3 is produced by conversion of T4 in tissues. The adrenal cortex makes cortisol under ACTH, aldosterone under the renin-angiotensin system and potassium, and androgens. Cortisol supports glucose production and stress responses. The adrenal medulla releases catecholamines (adrenaline and noradrenaline). Excess or deficiency changes metabolism, blood pressure and growth, so interpret results with the whole axis in mind.

sections.heading: Pancreas and calcium
sections.text: Pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin, which lowers blood glucose and promotes storage; alpha cells secrete glucagon, which raises glucose. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises plasma calcium by acting on bone, kidney and vitamin D activation. Calcitonin lowers calcium but is less important in adult humans. Calcium balance depends on PTH, vitamin D and phosphate. Feedback keeps these variables near set points, but reference ranges differ by laboratory and country; check local guidance.

keyPoints: Peptide hormones and amines such as adrenaline act on surface receptors, while steroid and thyroid hormones act on intracellular receptors and change gene transcription.
Only free hormone is active; bound hormone is a reserve, and free hormone = total hormone × free fraction.
Hypothalamic-pituitary axes use releasing hormones, stimulating hormones and negative feedback from target glands.
Thyroid hormones raise metabolic rate, cortisol supports glucose production and stress responses, and aldosterone controls sodium and potassium.
Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it; parathyroid hormone raises plasma calcium, while calcitonin lowers it.
Reference ranges and clinical guidance differ by laboratory and country, so check current local sources.

en.title: Sensory neurophysiology
en.short: Receptors, transduction, coding, sensory pathways and cortical maps.

sections.heading: Receptors and coding
sections.text: Sensory receptors convert stimuli into receptor potentials, graded membrane changes. If threshold is reached, action potentials travel along afferent axons. Receptors include mechanoreceptors, nociceptors, photoreceptors, hair cells and chemoreceptors. Transduction is this conversion. Coding covers modality, location, intensity and duration. Modality uses labelled lines, meaning each pathway carries one modality. Location uses receptive fields, the areas whose stimulation changes a neuron’s firing, and maps. Intensity uses firing rate and receptor recruitment. Duration uses adaptation, the decline in firing during a sustained stimulus. Tonic receptors fire throughout; phasic receptors fire mainly when a stimulus changes, as when clothing is noticed only when put on.

sections.heading: Main sensory pathways
sections.text: Somatosensory touch and proprioception pass through dorsal root ganglia and dorsal columns, cross in the medulla, and ascend via the medial lemniscus to thalamus and somatosensory cortex. Pain and temperature use the spinothalamic tract; the face uses trigeminal pathways. Vision starts in retinal photoreceptors, then bipolar and ganglion cells; axons cross partly at the chiasm and reach the lateral geniculate nucleus and visual cortex. Hearing uses cochlear hair cells, the cochlear nerve, brainstem nuclei, medial geniculate nucleus and auditory cortex. Vestibular hair cells signal via the vestibular nerve to vestibular nuclei, which connect to the cerebellum and cortex. Taste uses cranial nerves VII, IX and X, which synapse in the solitary nucleus, then relay through the thalamus to the insula. Smell uses olfactory receptor neurons to the olfactory bulb and cortex, with little thalamic relay.

sections.heading: Sensory cortex
sections.text: Primary sensory cortices contain topographic maps: the somatosensory homunculus (a distorted body map), retinotopic visual maps and tonotopic auditory maps. Cortical neurons have receptive fields and respond best to particular features. Processing is hierarchical and parallel, with separate streams for different features. Maps are plastic; use and injury can reshape them. Central adaptation also reduces perception of repeated stimuli, helping us notice change rather than constant background.

keyPoints: Sensory receptors transduce stimuli into graded receptor potentials; threshold leads to action potentials.
Coding uses labelled lines for modality, receptive fields and maps for location, firing rate and recruitment for intensity, and adaptation for duration.
Touch and proprioception use the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway; pain and temperature use the spinothalamic tract.
Vision relays through retina, lateral geniculate nucleus and visual cortex; hearing through cochlear hair cells, brainstem and auditory cortex.
Taste relays via thalamus to insula, while smell reaches the olfactory bulb and cortex with little thalamic relay.
Primary sensory cortices contain topographic maps and show hierarchical, parallel and plastic processing.

en.title: Motor control and neural integration
en.short: Reflexes, motor units, posture, voluntary movement, cerebellum, basal ganglia, sleep and cortex.

sections.heading: Reflexes and motor units
sections.text:
A motor unit is one alpha motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it supplies. Small units give fine control, as in eye muscles; large units give force, as in leg muscles.

A reflex is a stereotyped response to a stimulus. The stretch reflex, tested by tapping a tendon, uses muscle spindles that signal muscle length. The signal travels to the spinal cord, where alpha motor neurons fire and the muscle contracts. Reciprocal inhibition relaxes the opposing muscle. Golgi tendon organs sense tension and help limit force. Reflexes are fast but can be modified by descending signals.

sections.heading: Posture and voluntary movement
sections.text:
Posture is the background holding of the body against gravity. It depends on proprioception, the sense of body position, vestibular input and postural tone, with brainstem pathways setting the tone.

Voluntary movement begins with intention in association cortex, then premotor and supplementary motor areas plan sequences. The primary motor cortex sends commands down the corticospinal tract to alpha motor neurons. The map of the body on the cortex is the motor homunculus. Case: after stepping off a kerb, a student’s stretch reflex and postural adjustments act before conscious correction.

sections.heading: Cerebellum and basal ganglia
sections.text:
The cerebellum compares intended with actual movement, using sensory feedback. It corrects timing, smoothness and balance, and supports motor learning. It does not start movement.

The basal ganglia select wanted movements and suppress unwanted ones through direct and indirect pathways. In Parkinson’s disease, loss of dopamine causes slowness and rigidity. In Huntington’s disease, degeneration of striatal neurons causes unwanted movements called chorea.

sections.heading: Brainstem, sleep and cortex
sections.text:
The brainstem contains vestibular and reticular nuclei for posture, eye and head control. The reticular activating system maintains arousal and wakefulness.

Sleep has non-REM and REM stages, controlled by hypothalamic and brainstem circuits and circadian rhythm. Higher cortical functions include attention, working memory, language and planning, carried out by association cortex. These abilities depend on integrated networks, not one centre.

keyPoints: A motor unit is one alpha motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it innervates.
The stretch reflex uses muscle spindles and is modified by descending pathways.
Posture is maintained by brainstem and spinal circuits using proprioceptive and vestibular input.
The cerebellum coordinates timing and balance but does not initiate movement.
The basal ganglia select wanted movements and suppress unwanted ones.
Sleep, arousal and higher cortical functions depend on integrated brainstem, hypothalamic and cortical networks.

en.title: Autonomic nervous system
en.short: Sympathetic and parasympathetic wiring, transmitters, receptors, autonomic reflexes and the enteric nervous system.

sections.heading: Divisions and wiring
sections.text: The autonomic nervous system (ANS) controls involuntary functions: heart rate, vessel width, gut activity, bladder emptying, pupil size and sweating. It has sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions plus the enteric nervous system. Sympathetic preganglionic neurons leave the thoracolumbar spinal cord and synapse in ganglia. Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons leave through cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X and sacral segments S2 to S4. Both divisions use a preganglionic neuron and a postganglionic neuron in series.

sections.heading: Transmitters and receptors
sections.text: All preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine (ACh), which acts on nicotinic receptors in ganglia. Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release noradrenaline onto alpha or beta adrenergic receptors. Exceptions: sympathetic fibres to sweat glands release ACh onto muscarinic receptors, and the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and noradrenaline into blood. Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release ACh onto muscarinic receptors. Location explains effects: beta1 in heart raises rate and force; alpha1 in vessels constricts; M2 in heart slows it; M3 mediates contraction in gut and bladder smooth muscle and the pupil constrictor.

sections.heading: Reflex control
sections.text: Autonomic reflexes adjust organs without conscious control. In the baroreceptor reflex, stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch sense blood pressure. A fall in pressure reduces their firing, so sympathetic outflow rises and vagal tone falls. Heart rate and force increase, and vessels constrict. For example, Amina stands up quickly; her blood pressure dips briefly, the reflex raises her heart rate, and she may feel light-headed. The bladder stores urine under sympathetic beta3 relaxation and alpha1 sphincter contraction; parasympathetic M3 contracts the detrusor during voiding. Pupils dilate through sympathetic alpha1 and constrict through parasympathetic M3. Sweat glands are sympathetic but cholinergic.

sections.heading: Enteric nervous system
sections.text: The enteric nervous system is a mesh of neurons in the gut wall. The myenteric plexus controls motility, and the submucosal plexus controls secretion and blood flow. It can work locally, but sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves modulate it. This is physiology, not treatment advice; check current national or WHO guidance for clinical rules.

keyPoints: The ANS has sympathetic, parasympathetic and enteric divisions and controls involuntary organs.
All preganglionic autonomic neurons release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors.
Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release noradrenaline onto alpha or beta receptors; sweat glands are a cholinergic exception.
Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors.
The baroreceptor reflex raises sympathetic outflow and lowers vagal tone when blood pressure falls.
The enteric nervous system can act locally but is modulated by autonomic nerves.

en.title: Haemostasis and blood transfusion physiology
en.short: Platelets, clotting, fibrinolysis, blood groups, cross-matching and transfusion reactions.

sections.heading: Vascular and platelet phase
sections.text: Haemostasis is the controlled stopping of bleeding while blood stays fluid elsewhere. Injured vessels constrict. Platelets adhere to exposed collagen through von Willebrand factor, become activated, change shape and release ADP and thromboxane A2. These recruit more platelets. Aggregation uses glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors, which bind fibrinogen and link platelets into a temporary plug. Endothelial nitric oxide and prostacyclin limit the plug to the injury site.

sections.heading: Coagulation and fibrinolysis
sections.text: Coagulation strengthens the plug with fibrin. The classical cascade has extrinsic, intrinsic and common pathways, but in vivo clotting is cell-based and starts mainly with tissue factor and factor VII. The common pathway activates factor X, then thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin and activates factor XIII to cross-link it. Factors II, VII, IX and X need vitamin K; calcium is required. Antithrombin, protein C, protein S and tissue factor pathway inhibitor restrain clotting. In fibrinolysis, tissue plasminogen activator converts plasminogen to plasmin, which digests fibrin; fibrin degradation products include D-dimers.

sections.heading: Blood groups and cross-matching
sections.text: Blood groups are inherited red cell antigens. ABO typing identifies A and B antigens; plasma contains antibodies against absent antigens, so group A has anti-B. Rh D is the main antigen in the Rh system. Cross-matching principles are: confirm ABO and Rh D, screen for unexpected antibodies, then cross-match donor cells with recipient serum, or use a validated electronic system. A compatible unit shows no reaction in the cross-match.

sections.heading: Transfusion reactions
sections.text: Transfusion reactions arise from immune or non-immune causes. Acute haemolytic reaction follows ABO incompatibility: recipient antibodies bind donor red cells, complement causes intravascular haemolysis, and fever, flank pain, hypotension and haemoglobinuria may follow. Other types include febrile non-haemolytic, allergic, anaphylactic, transfusion-associated circulatory overload, transfusion-related acute lung injury and delayed haemolysis. Case: a group A patient given group B red cells has anti-B antibodies that destroy the donor cells. Stop the transfusion and follow local emergency guidance. Policies differ by country; check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Haemostasis has vascular, platelet and coagulation phases, balanced by anticoagulant and fibrinolytic controls.
Platelets adhere via von Willebrand factor, activate and aggregate through glycoprotein IIb/IIIa and fibrinogen.
Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin; vitamin K is needed for factors II, VII, IX and X.
Plasmin digests fibrin, producing D-dimers, and is generated from plasminogen by tissue plasminogen activator.
ABO antibodies attack antigens the person lacks; Rh D is the main Rh antigen.
Cross-matching checks ABO and Rh D, antibody screen and donor-recipient compatibility; acute haemolytic reaction is usually ABO incompatibility.

en.title: Immune physiology and body defence
en.short: Innate and adaptive immunity, antibodies, complement, cytokines, inflammation and fever.

sections.heading: Innate immunity
sections.text: Innate immunity is the fast, non-specific first line. Barriers such as skin and mucus stop entry. If microbes enter, macrophages and neutrophils engulf them by phagocytosis, and natural killer cells destroy infected cells. Innate cells recognise shared microbial patterns through pattern recognition receptors. It acts within minutes to hours and does not improve with repeated exposure. Dendritic cells then carry antigen to lymph nodes, linking innate to adaptive defence.

sections.heading: Adaptive immunity
sections.text: Adaptive immunity is specific and slow on first contact, but creates memory. An antigen is any molecule the immune system recognises. B lymphocytes make antibodies (immunoglobulins); T lymphocytes kill infected cells (cytotoxic) or help other cells (helper). Antibodies bind antigen, neutralise toxins and viruses, and mark microbes for destruction. Memory cells make the second response faster and stronger, which is the basis of vaccination.

sections.heading: Complement and cytokines
sections.text: Complement is a group of plasma proteins that act in a cascade. It opsonises microbes (marks them for phagocytosis), attracts phagocytes, and can punch holes in bacterial membranes. Cytokines are small signalling proteins: interleukins, interferons and tumour necrosis factor. They coordinate cell movement and inflammation. Trafficking is guided by chemokines and adhesion molecules, which let white cells stick to vessel walls and migrate into tissue.

sections.heading: Inflammation and fever
sections.text: Inflammation is the local response to injury or infection: redness, heat, swelling, pain and lost function. Vasodilation and increased permeability bring cells and protein-rich fluid. Fever is a raised body temperature set point driven by cytokines such as interleukin-1 acting on the hypothalamus. The neuroendocrine system also responds: cortisol from the adrenal cortex suppresses immune activity, and the vagus nerve signals the brain. For example, a child with a bacterial throat infection develops fever and a raised white cell count; these are signs, not diagnoses.

keyPoints: Innate immunity is fast and non-specific; adaptive immunity is specific and forms memory.
An antigen is a molecule recognised by the immune system; an antibody is a protein made by B cells that binds it.
Complement opsonises microbes, attracts phagocytes and can lyse bacterial membranes.
Cytokines and adhesion molecules direct immune cell trafficking into tissues.
Fever is a cytokine-driven rise in the hypothalamic set point, not simply overheating.
Cortisol and autonomic nerve signals link immune activity to the neuroendocrine system.

en.title: Reproductive physiology
en.short: Gonadal function, gametogenesis, sex steroids, HPG axis, menstrual cycle, pregnancy, lactation, male fertility.

sections.heading: Gonads and gametes
sections.text: Gonads are the testes and ovaries. They produce gametes by gametogenesis and secrete sex steroids. Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so gametes are haploid. Spermatogenesis starts at puberty and is continuous. Oogenesis starts before birth, pauses in prophase I, completes meiosis I at ovulation and meiosis II at fertilisation. Sex steroids are fat-soluble: they enter cells, bind nuclear receptors and act as transcription factors, altering protein synthesis. Testosterone drives male development; oestradiol and progesterone act on female reproductive tissues.

sections.heading: HPG axis and cycle
sections.text: The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis links brain and gonads. Hypothalamic GnRH (gonadotrophin-releasing hormone) makes the anterior pituitary release FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) and LH (luteinising hormone). FSH supports ovarian follicles and testicular Sertoli cells; LH triggers ovulation and Leydig cell testosterone. Steroids and inhibin feed back negatively. In a 28-day model, FSH recruits follicles and rising oestradiol thickens the endometrium. An oestradiol surge triggers the LH surge, so ovulation occurs near day 14. The ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone to maintain the endometrium. If pregnancy does not occur it regresses, progesterone falls and menstruation follows.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, lactation, male function
sections.text: After fertilisation the trophoblast secretes hCG (human chorionic gonadotrophin), which keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone until the placenta takes over. Prolactin promotes milk synthesis; oxytocin causes myoepithelial contraction for milk ejection. In men, FSH and testosterone support spermatogenesis, and LH maintains testosterone. Case: a student notes that a man given exogenous testosterone may become infertile, because negative feedback lowers GnRH, FSH and LH, reducing intratesticular testosterone and sperm production.

keyPoints: Gonads make gametes by meiosis and secrete sex steroids.
Spermatogenesis is continuous from puberty; oogenesis pauses in prophase I until ovulation.
GnRH drives FSH and LH release; steroids and inhibin feed back negatively.
An oestradiol surge triggers the LH surge and ovulation near day 14.
The corpus luteum secretes progesterone; hCG maintains it in early pregnancy.
Prolactin makes milk; oxytocin ejects it.

en.title: Thermoregulation and exercise physiology
en.short: Heat balance, hypothalamic control, acclimatisation, and exercise responses, fatigue and limits.

sections.heading: Heat balance and control
sections.text: Thermoregulation keeps core temperature near a set point, about 37 °C. Heat comes mainly from metabolism, especially contracting muscle, and is lost by radiation, conduction, convection and evaporation. In heat and during exercise, sweating is the main heat-loss route, but it works only when sweat evaporates; humidity limits it. The hypothalamus compares blood temperature with the set point. When temperature rises, it increases sweating and skin blood flow and reduces heat production. When it falls, it causes vasoconstriction and shivering.

sections.heading: Acclimatisation and example
sections.text: Repeated heat exposure over days to weeks produces acclimatisation: sweating starts earlier and is more dilute, plasma volume rises, and cardiovascular stability improves. Worked example: a cyclist uses 800 W of metabolic power and performs 200 W of external work, so efficiency is 200 ÷ 800 × 100 = 25%. The other 600 W becomes heat. If evaporation removes 500 W and other losses are negligible, storage is 100 W. For 10 minutes, stored energy is 100 × 600 = 60,000 J. With specific heat 3.47 kJ per kg per °C, a 70 kg person’s rise is 60,000 ÷ (70 × 3,470) = 0.25 °C.

sections.heading: Exercise responses
sections.text: During exercise, cardiac output rises through higher heart rate and stroke volume. Blood flow shifts from inactive organs to working muscle and skin. Ventilation rises to meet gas exchange. Oxygen consumption (VO2) rises with work rate until a plateau, maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max), which limits endurance performance. Short bursts use phosphocreatine and anaerobic glycolysis; longer work depends more on oxidative phosphorylation.

sections.heading: Fatigue and limits
sections.text: Fatigue is the inability to maintain the expected force or power output. It has central causes, such as reduced brain drive, and peripheral causes, such as fuel depletion and metabolite accumulation in muscle. Limits depend on event duration: sprinting on phosphocreatine and anaerobic capacity, middle-distance events on mixed contributions, and long events on oxygen delivery, fuel, heat and hydration. Lactate is a fuel and signal; the lactate threshold is the intensity above which lactate production exceeds clearance and blood lactate starts to rise.

keyPoints: Core temperature is controlled by the hypothalamus through sweating, skin blood flow, shivering and heat production.
Heat is lost by radiation, conduction, convection and evaporation; sweat evaporation is limited in high humidity.
Acclimatisation improves sweating and cardiovascular stability after repeated heat exposure.
Exercise raises cardiac output, ventilation and oxygen consumption; VO2max sets an endurance ceiling.
Mechanical efficiency = external work ÷ metabolic energy × 100; heat storage = heat production − heat loss.
Fatigue has central and peripheral causes, and the lactate threshold marks where lactate production exceeds clearance.

en.title: Integrative physiology and adaptation
en.short: How systems integrate in haemorrhage, dehydration, starvation, altitude and stress.

sections.heading: Integration and control
sections.text: Integrative physiology studies how systems act together. A challenge changes several variables at once. Control systems use sensors, afferent pathways, integrating centres and effectors. Negative feedback opposes the change; feedforward anticipates it. Nerve reflexes act in seconds, hormones in minutes to hours, and tissue adaptation over days to weeks. Redundancy means several systems defend one variable, such as blood pressure. Trade-offs occur because defending one variable can disturb another.

sections.heading: Haemorrhage
sections.text: In haemorrhage, falling blood volume lowers venous return and stroke volume. Arterial baroreceptors (pressure sensors) reduce firing, so sympathetic outflow rises and vagal tone falls. Heart rate and contractility increase, and arterioles and veins constrict. This defends mean arterial pressure, but vasoconstriction reduces flow to skin, gut and kidney. Capillary pressure falls, so interstitial fluid enters capillaries. Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone conserve salt and water, and thirst increases intake. Erythropoietin supports red cell production later. For example, a 60 kg adult has about 4.2 L blood at 70 mL/kg. Losing 1 L is about 24 per cent.

sections.heading: Dehydration and starvation
sections.text: Dehydration raises plasma osmolality. Hypothalamic osmoreceptors (osmolality sensors) trigger antidiuretic hormone release and thirst. The kidney concentrates urine, and aldosterone conserves sodium. If loss is severe, blood pressure falls and the baroreflex and hormonal systems act. Starvation differs: low insulin and high glucagon promote glycogen breakdown and new glucose formation, then fat oxidation and ketone formation. The brain uses glucose and, in prolonged starvation, ketones. Protein is spared, but lean tissue is lost.

sections.heading: Altitude and stress
sections.text: At altitude, low partial pressure of oxygen reduces arterial oxygen content. Oxygen sensors increase ventilation within seconds. The resulting alkaline blood from overbreathing is corrected by renal bicarbonate excretion over days. Erythropoietin raises red cell mass over weeks, and tissues increase capillaries and mitochondria. Stress activates the sympathetic nervous system and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. Cortisol raises glucose availability and moderates inflammation, while catecholamines support blood pressure and alertness. These responses help survival but can harm. Management follows national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Integration means several control systems defend blood pressure, oxygen delivery and fluid balance together.
Haemorrhage triggers baroreflex, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, antidiuretic hormone and thirst responses, with erythropoietin acting later.
At 70 mL/kg, a 60 kg adult has about 4.2 L blood; losing 1 L is about 24 per cent.
Dehydration raises osmolality, so antidiuretic hormone and thirst conserve water while aldosterone conserves sodium.
Starvation shifts fuel use from glycogen and glucose to fat and ketones, sparing protein where possible.
Altitude and stress combine rapid neural reflexes with slower hormonal and tissue adaptation, and prolonged responses can cause harm.

en.title: Physiology laboratory methods and research ethics
en.short: Safe measurement, calibration, quality control and ethical conduct in physiology laboratories.

sections.heading: Safe measurement
sections.text: Before recording any physiological variable, define the purpose and choose the least invasive method. For cardiovascular work, let the person rest, use the correct cuff size for blood pressure, and clean and dry the skin before applying ECG electrodes. Do not test someone alone if they have a known heart condition. For respiratory tests such as spirometry, check for recent surgery or acute illness, use a clean mouthpiece and filter, and watch for dizziness.
