For nerve and muscle tests such as electromyography (EMG), prepare the skin, check electrode impedance, and use the lowest stimulus that gives a clear response. Stop if the person feels unwell.

sections.heading: Calibration and quality control
sections.text: Calibration means comparing an instrument with a known standard. Record the gain, time base (sweep speed) and filter settings. A simple example: an ECG amplifier set to 10 mm per millivolt deflects 10 mm for a 1 mV calibration pulse. If an unknown signal deflects 25 mm, its size is 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5 mV. Quality control includes daily checks, duplicate readings, and records of who measured, when, and with what settings. Keep equipment logs and report faults.

sections.heading: Human participants
sections.text: Human studies need approval from an independent research ethics committee before any measurement. Informed consent means explaining purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, confidentiality and the right to withdraw without penalty. Use at least two identifiers, store data securely, and anonymise, meaning remove names and identifying details, where possible. A student who records classmates’ blood pressure for a class project still needs consent and a data plan. National data protection laws differ, so follow the current local rule.

sections.heading: Animals and data
sections.text: Animal work requires ethics approval, trained staff, humane endpoints (pre-agreed points at which an animal is removed from a study to prevent suffering) and the 3Rs: replacement, reduction and refinement. Keep records of anaesthesia and monitoring. For all data, define who may access files, keep backups, and retain records for the period required by your institution. The Declaration of Helsinki is a key international statement on human research ethics; you must also follow local laws and your ethics committee’s rules.

keyPoints: Choose the least invasive method and stop if the participant becomes unwell.
Calibrate with a known standard and record gain, time base and filter settings.
Signal size = deflection ÷ gain; at 10 mm/mV, a 25 mm deflection is 2.5 mV.
Quality control uses duplicate readings, equipment logs and fault reporting.
Human research needs ethics approval, informed consent and secure data handling.
Animal research follows the 3Rs and needs approval, training and humane endpoints.

en.title: Applied physiology: systems in health and disease
en.short: How cardiovascular, respiratory, renal and endocrine mechanisms interact in shock, oedema, anaemia and diabetes.

sections.heading: Shock as system failure
sections.text: Shock is circulatory failure that leaves tissues underperfused. It may follow blood loss (hypovolaemic), pump failure (cardiogenic), vasodilation (distributive) or obstruction to filling (obstructive). Baroreceptors sense low pressure and raise sympathetic tone, so the pulse is fast and skin may be cool. The kidneys retain sodium and water through renin, angiotensin and aldosterone. Antidiuretic hormone conserves water. Signs include low blood pressure, confusion and low urine output. Respiratory compensation for acidosis increases breathing. Management follows national or WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Oedema and Starling forces
sections.text: Oedema is excess interstitial fluid. Capillary Starling forces govern it: hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, plasma oncotic pressure pulls it in, and capillary permeability and lymphatic drainage set the balance. Heart failure raises venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure. Hypoalbuminaemia lowers oncotic pressure. Inflammation increases permeability. The kidneys worsen retention by conserving sodium. Signs are swelling, rapid weight gain and, if fluid fills the lungs, breathlessness.

sections.heading: Anaemia and oxygen delivery
sections.text: Anaemia is a low haemoglobin concentration, so arterial oxygen content falls. Oxygen delivery is cardiac output times arterial oxygen content. The body compensates with tachycardia, higher cardiac output and a right shift of the haemoglobin curve. The kidneys release erythropoietin. A person with haemoglobin 70 g/L and saturation 0.98 carries about 92 mL oxygen per litre (1.34 × 70 × 0.98), against 138 mL/L at 105 g/L. Pallor, fatigue and breathlessness reflect reduced delivery.

sections.heading: Diabetes across systems
sections.text: Diabetes is chronic hyperglycaemia from insulin deficiency, insulin resistance or both. Without insulin, glucose stays in the blood and acts as an osmotic load. The kidneys cannot reabsorb it all, so glucose appears in urine and pulls water with it, causing polyuria, thirst and dehydration. Potassium and sodium are lost. In type 1 diabetes, fat breakdown produces ketones and acidosis. Over years, high glucose damages blood vessels and nerves, affecting the heart, kidneys and eyes. Clinical care must follow national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion; types reflect blood loss, pump failure, vasodilation or obstruction.
Oedema results from altered Starling forces, increased permeability or poor lymphatic drainage, often worsened by renal sodium retention.
Oxygen delivery = cardiac output × arterial oxygen content; anaemia lowers content and triggers cardiovascular and erythropoietin compensation.
In diabetes, hyperglycaemia causes osmotic diuresis and dehydration; type 1 also causes ketosis.
Signs reflect mechanisms: fast pulse and low urine output in shock, swelling and breathlessness in oedema, pallor and fatigue in anaemia, polyuria and thirst in diabetes.
Clinical management must follow current national or WHO guidance; this summary explains mechanisms, not treatment protocols.

en.title: Advanced systems physiology: integration and control
en.short: Covers organ interaction, transport, feedback and integrated cardiovascular, respiratory, renal and endocrine models.

sections.heading: Transport and balance
sections.text: Models treat the body as compartments linked by flows. The mass balance equation is accumulation = input − output + production − consumption. At steady state, input plus production equals output plus consumption. The Fick principle states that uptake of a substance equals blood flow times the arteriovenous concentration difference. For oxygen, if cardiac output is 5 L/min, arterial oxygen content is 200 mL/L and venous content is 150 mL/L, oxygen uptake is 5 × (200 − 150) = 250 mL/min. Renal clearance = (urine concentration × urine flow) / plasma concentration. If urine inulin is 100 mg/dL, urine flow 1 mL/min and plasma inulin 1 mg/dL, clearance is 100 × 1 / 1 = 100 mL/min.

sections.heading: Feedback and control
sections.text: Control theory describes how a system holds a variable near a set point. Negative feedback compares the measured value with the set point, giving an error e = set point − measured value. The controller produces a response proportional to the error, response = K × e, where K is gain. High gain corrects small errors but can destabilise a system with delay. A time constant describes how quickly a compartment responds. Endocrine axes, such as thyroid and adrenal axes, use negative feedback; the hypothalamus and pituitary sense hormone levels and adjust output. Models test whether a proposed loop can explain observed stability or oscillation.

sections.heading: Integrated models
sections.text: Integrated models link cardiovascular, respiratory, renal and endocrine subsystems. Oxygen delivery is cardiac output times arterial oxygen content; it must match tissue demand. Carbon dioxide removal depends on alveolar ventilation and pulmonary blood flow. The kidney regulates sodium and water, and so plasma volume and blood pressure, while endocrine signals such as aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone adjust renal transport. A useful model states its assumptions, parameters and validation data. Sensitivity analysis shows which parameter most affects the output. Models support understanding and research; they do not replace measurement, and clinical decisions follow current WHO or national guidance.

keyPoints: Mass balance: accumulation = input − output + production − consumption; at steady state input plus production equals output plus consumption.
Fick principle: uptake = blood flow × arteriovenous concentration difference.
Renal clearance = (urine concentration × urine flow) / plasma concentration; units must match.
Negative feedback error e = set point − measured value; response = K × e, where K is gain.
High gain with delay can destabilise a control loop; time constants describe response speed.
Integrated models link cardiovascular, respiratory, renal and endocrine systems, but must state assumptions and be validated against data.

en.title: Research methods in physiology
en.short: Questions, designs, sampling, measurement, inference, reporting, ethics and dissertation planning.

sections.heading: Questions and designs
sections.text: A good research question names the population, exposure or intervention, comparator, outcome and time frame. It must be feasible. Experimental designs manipulate a factor, ideally with randomisation and controls, to support causal claims. Observational designs do not manipulate: cross-sectional studies measure at one time, cohort studies follow people forward, and case-control studies compare past exposures in people with and without an outcome. Confounding is a third factor that influences both exposure and outcome.

sections.heading: Sampling and measurement
sections.text: Sampling is selecting participants from a defined population. Probability sampling, which gives each member of the population a known chance of selection, supports generalisation; convenience sampling limits it. Measurement validity means an instrument measures what it claims. Reliability is consistency; calibration checks against a standard. Bias is systematic error. Example: a student in Ibadan studies resting heart rate before and after a 12-week exercise programme in 40 adults. She uses one calibrated monitor and blinded analysis. Mean change is 4 beats/min, SD 8. Standard error = 8 ÷ √40 = 1.26; 95% CI ≈ 4 ± 2.02 × 1.26 = 1.4 to 6.6 beats/min.

sections.heading: Inference and reporting
sections.text: Statistical inference uses sample data to estimate population values or test hypotheses. A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme if the null hypothesis is true; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true. Confidence intervals show estimate precision. Type I error is a false positive; type II error is a false negative; power is the chance of detecting a real effect. Pre-specify outcomes and analysis, report all results, and follow reporting guidelines such as CONSORT for trials and STROBE for observational studies.

sections.heading: Ethics, data and planning
sections.text: Research ethics requires ethics committee approval, informed consent, confidentiality and fair selection. Animal studies need humane care and approval. Data management includes a data dictionary that defines each variable, secure storage, anonymisation, backups and reproducible analysis. For a dissertation, agree the question with your supervisor early, check feasibility and sample size, pilot the methods, keep a timeline, and write the protocol before collecting data. Rules differ by country and institution; check current local requirements.

keyPoints: A strong research question states population, exposure or intervention, comparator, outcome and time frame.
Experimental designs manipulate a factor with randomisation and controls; observational designs do not.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; convenience sampling limits it.
Validity is measuring what is claimed; reliability is consistency; bias is systematic error.
Standard error = standard deviation ÷ √n; a 95% confidence interval is roughly estimate ± 2 standard errors in large samples.
Pre-specify analysis, report all outcomes, obtain ethics approval and manage data securely.

en.title: Computational and systems physiology
en.short: Dynamic models, simulation, parameter estimation, validation and sensitivity analysis in physiology.

sections.heading: Models and simulation
sections.text: A dynamic model describes how physiological state variables change with time. State variables are the quantities tracked, such as concentration or volume. Parameters are fixed constants in the equations. A common form is an ordinary differential equation (ODE). For a single compartment: dC/dt = k_in − k_out × C. Here k_in is input rate and k_out is the rate constant for removal. Simulation solves such equations numerically or analytically. If k_in = 2 units/min and k_out = 0.5/min, steady state C_ss = k_in/k_out = 4 units. The time constant, the time to reach about 63% of steady state, is τ = 1/k_out = 2 min. Starting from zero, C at 2 min is 4(1 − e^−1) = 2.53 units.

sections.heading: Parameter estimation
sections.text: Parameter estimation finds parameter values that make model output agree with experimental data. A common method minimises the sum of squared differences between predictions and observations, or uses a likelihood, which scores how probable the data are under the model, when noise is included. Estimates should come with uncertainty, such as confidence intervals. Identifiability asks whether the data can distinguish parameter values. Poor identifiability means different parameter values can fit the data equally well, and overfitting produces models that fit one dataset but fail on new data. Report units and fitting assumptions. A good fit does not prove the model is correct.

sections.heading: Validation and sensitivity
sections.text: Validation tests whether a model predicts independent data, not merely the data used for fitting. Sensitivity analysis asks how outputs respond to parameter changes. Local sensitivity varies one parameter at a time; global methods vary many together. Sensitive parameters deserve careful measurement. Interpretation must combine simulation with experimental evidence: a model is a hypothesis, not proof. Computational physiology supports experiment design and explains mechanisms, but conclusions depend on model structure, parameter uncertainty and the data used.

keyPoints: A dynamic model tracks state variables over time using equations such as dC/dt = k_in − k_out × C.
Simulation solves model equations; for that model C_ss = k_in/k_out and τ = 1/k_out.
Parameter estimation fits parameters to data, and estimates need uncertainty and identifiability checks.
Validation uses independent data; a good fit does not prove a model is correct.
Sensitivity analysis shows which parameters most affect outputs; local varies one at a time, global many together.
Computational models are hypotheses to interpret alongside experiments, not proof of mechanism.

en.title: Molecular and cellular physiology: specialist frontiers
en.short: Advanced transport, ion channels, signalling, imaging and research tools at molecular level.

sections.heading: Transport frontiers
sections.text: Advanced membrane transport asks how cells move solutes across barriers with speed and selectivity. Primary active transporters use ATP directly, such as the Na+/K+ ATPase. Secondary active transporters use the electrochemical gradient made by those pumps, coupling one solute down its gradient to another up its gradient. Epithelial cells place different transporters on apical and basolateral membranes, so transport becomes directional. Research now links transporter structure to disease and to drug targeting.

sections.heading: Channels and signals
sections.text: Ion channels are membrane proteins with a pore, a selectivity filter and gates that open in response to voltage, ligands or mechanical force. Structure-function work uses cryo-electron microscopy and mutagenesis to map these parts. A mutation may change gating or selectivity and cause a channelopathy. Signal transduction converts an extracellular signal into a cellular response. Receptors activate G proteins or kinases, producing second messengers such as cAMP or calcium. The same signal can differ between cell types because of the proteins expressed.

sections.heading: Imaging and control
sections.text: Cellular imaging shows where molecules are and when signals change. Fluorescent proteins, calcium indicators and super-resolution microscopy allow live cells to be studied, though light can damage them and labels can alter behaviour. Optogenetics uses light-sensitive proteins, such as channelrhodopsin, to switch defined cells on or off with light. It is powerful in animal research but needs careful controls and ethical review.

sections.heading: Research strategies
sections.text: Patch clamp records currents through single channels or the whole cell, giving direct tests of channel behaviour. For example, if 1,000 channels each carry 2 pA (picoamperes) when open and open probability is 0.05, whole-cell current is 1,000 × 2 pA × 0.05 = 100 pA. Omics methods measure many genes, proteins or metabolites at once; they generate hypotheses rather than proof. Strong studies combine these tools, validate findings across models, and report limitations.

keyPoints: Primary active transport uses ATP; secondary active transport uses an electrochemical gradient.
Ion channels have a pore, selectivity filter and gating mechanism; mutations can cause channelopathies.
Signal transduction uses receptors, G proteins, kinases and second messengers such as cAMP and calcium.
Patch clamp measures single-channel or whole-cell currents; whole-cell current = channel number × single-channel current × open probability.
Optogenetics uses light-sensitive proteins to control cell activity, with controls and ethics required.
Omics screens many molecules at once and needs validation; imaging must consider photodamage and label artefacts.
